Genesis.author: Moses (traditional)
Genesis.date: c. 1400 BC (or 5th c. BC in critical scholarship)
Genesis.overview: Genesis answers the foundational questions: Where did everything come from? Why is there evil? How did Israel begin? It traces God's purposes from creation through the lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, establishing the covenant promises that drive the rest of Scripture.

Exodus.author: Moses (traditional)
Exodus.overview: Exodus records Israel's liberation from Egyptian slavery and the birth of the nation at Sinai. The giving of the Torah and the construction of the Tabernacle reveal that God's ultimate goal is not just freedom but dwelling with his people.

Leviticus.author: Moses (traditional)
Leviticus.overview: Leviticus is the handbook for Israel's worship, detailing sacrificial laws, priestly duties, and the annual calendar of feasts. Its central refrain — 'Be holy, because I am holy' — shaped Israel's entire life as a covenant people set apart for God.

Numbers.author: Moses (traditional)
Numbers.overview: Numbers covers Israel's forty years in the wilderness, bookended by two census counts. It honestly records a generation's failure to trust God, yet also God's persistent faithfulness in keeping his covenant despite repeated rebellion.

Deuteronomy.author: Moses (traditional)
Deuteronomy.overview: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell address on the plains of Moab, renewing the Sinai covenant with the second generation before they enter Canaan. Its call to love God with heart, soul, and strength (6:4-5) became the heartbeat of Jewish faith and was cited by Jesus as the greatest commandment.

Joshua.author: Joshua / later editor
Joshua.overview: Joshua records the fulfilment of God's four-century-old promise of land, as Israel enters and settles Canaan under Joshua's leadership. The book wrestles with the tension between God's total faithfulness and Israel's partial obedience.

Judges.author: Unknown (possibly Samuel)
Judges.overview: Judges traces a grim downward spiral — Israel sins, suffers, cries out, is delivered by a judge, then repeats the cycle. Figures like Deborah, Gideon, and Samson reveal both God's grace and the chaos that results when 'everyone does what is right in their own eyes.'

Ruth.author: Unknown
Ruth.overview: Ruth is a gem of narrative art set in the time of the Judges, following a Moabite widow who clings to her Israelite mother-in-law and finds refuge under the wings of Israel's God. Its climax — Ruth's inclusion in the lineage of David and ultimately of Christ — makes it a story about the reach of covenant love.

1 Samuel.author: Unknown; possibly Samuel, Nathan, Gad
1 Samuel.overview: 1 Samuel narrates Israel's transition from tribal confederacy to monarchy, tracing the careers of Samuel, Saul, and the young David. It shows that Israel's desire for a king 'like the nations' both fulfilled and complicated God's purposes.

2 Samuel.author: Unknown
2 Samuel.overview: 2 Samuel follows David's reign — his triumphs in uniting Israel, the Davidic covenant promising an eternal throne, and his devastating moral failure with Bathsheba. The rest of the book shows how sin unravels a kingdom even as God's covenant faithfulness endures.

1 Kings.author: Unknown (traditionally Jeremiah)
1 Kings.overview: 1 Kings covers Solomon's magnificent reign — the Temple, his wisdom, his fall into idolatry — and then the tragic split of the kingdom under Rehoboam. Elijah emerges as the great prophetic voice of the northern kingdom's apostasy under Ahab.

2 Kings.author: Unknown (traditionally Jeremiah)
2 Kings.overview: 2 Kings traces the decline of both Israel (north) and Judah (south) through relentless apostasy, despite the ministry of prophets like Elisha. It ends with the catastrophe of Jerusalem's fall and the Babylonian exile — the covenant curses of Deuteronomy realized.

1 Chronicles.author: Traditionally Ezra
1 Chronicles.overview: Chronicles retells Israel's history from a priestly, post-exilic perspective. Written for returnees from Babylon, it focuses on David and the Temple to affirm that the covenant community still has a future — their identity is rooted in worship, not political power.

2 Chronicles.author: Traditionally Ezra
2 Chronicles.overview: 2 Chronicles continues from Solomon's Temple dedication through the exile, emphasizing the cycles of faithfulness, reform, and apostasy in Judah. It ends, uniquely, with Cyrus's decree allowing the exiles to return — a note of hope pointing to restoration.

Ezra.author: Traditionally Ezra
Ezra.overview: Ezra records two waves of return from Babylon and the rebuilding of the Temple (chapters 1–6) and Ezra's own arrival to teach the Torah (chapters 7–10). It wrestles with the question of what it means to be God's people after judgment.

Nehemiah.author: Traditionally Nehemiah
Nehemiah.overview: Nehemiah combines a personal memoir of courageous leadership with a community story of Jerusalem's walls being rebuilt in 52 days against fierce opposition. The climactic public reading of the Torah and covenant renewal show that the community's ultimate wall is Scripture.

Esther.author: Unknown
Esther.overview: Esther is famously the one biblical book that never names God, yet divine providence permeates every reversal of fortune. Set in the Persian court, it follows a Jewish queen who risks her life to save her people from genocide — a story of hidden sovereignty.

Job.author: Unknown
Job.date: Unknown; possibly patriarchal era or 5th c. BC
Job.overview: Job is the Bible's most sustained engagement with the problem of innocent suffering. The prose frame surrounds a poetic dialogue in which Job's friends insist suffering equals sin, while Job demands an audience with God — and God ultimately vindicates Job's honesty over his friends' tidy theology.

Psalms.author: David (73 psalms), Asaph, Sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, and others
Psalms.overview: The 150 Psalms are Israel's hymnbook and prayer book, spanning every human emotion from ecstatic praise to raw despair. Organized into five books mirroring the Pentateuch, they shaped Jewish worship for centuries and are the most-quoted OT book in the NT.

Proverbs.author: Solomon and others (Agur, Lemuel)
Proverbs.overview: Proverbs is practical wisdom for everyday life, rooted not in abstract philosophy but in 'the fear of the LORD.' It addresses speech, relationships, money, work, and character, presenting wisdom as a way of living that aligns with God's created order.

Ecclesiastes.author: Qoheleth ('the Teacher'); traditionally Solomon
Ecclesiastes.overview: Ecclesiastes is the Bible's most searingly honest book about the limits of human wisdom and the frustration of life 'under the sun.' The Teacher tests every avenue of meaning — work, pleasure, wisdom, wealth — and finds all of it hebel (vapor). Its conclusion: fear God, keep his commands, enjoy his gifts.

Song of Solomon.author: Traditionally Solomon
Song of Solomon.overview: The Song celebrates the beauty of romantic love and physical desire between a man and a woman, affirming that sexuality is God's good gift. Read across the centuries as an allegory of God's love for Israel or Christ's love for the church, it also stands as Israel's most frank affirmation of embodied human love.

Isaiah.author: Isaiah ben Amoz; critical scholarship posits multiple authors
Isaiah.date: c. 740–700 BC (chs. 1–39); c. 550–540 BC (chs. 40–66) per critical view
Isaiah.overview: Isaiah is the 'fifth gospel' of the OT — no prophet more fully anticipates the work of Jesus. Its first half thunders judgment against Israel and the nations; its second half opens with 'Comfort, comfort my people' and rises to the vision of a new heavens and new earth. The Servant Songs (42, 49, 50, 52–53) are the heart of NT Christology.

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah ben Hilkiah; Baruch served as his scribe
Jeremiah.overview: Jeremiah prophesied during Judah's final decades before the Babylonian exile, faithfully announcing judgment at enormous personal cost. His most luminous promise — a new covenant written on hearts, not stone — is quoted more extensively in the NT than any other OT passage (Heb 8:8-12).

Lamentations.author: Traditionally Jeremiah
Lamentations.overview: Five exquisitely crafted acrostic poems mourn the destruction of Jerusalem, giving voice to communal grief without flinching from the reality of divine judgment. At its center, amid the ruins, the poet declares: 'The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end.'

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel ben Buzi, priest
Ezekiel.overview: Ezekiel prophesied to the exiles in Babylon through overwhelming visions — the chariot-throne of God, the valley of dry bones, the new Temple. His central concern is God's honor and the vindication of his name among the nations through Israel's judgment and ultimate restoration.

Daniel.author: Traditionally Daniel
Daniel.date: 6th c. BC (traditional); 2nd c. BC per critical scholarship
Daniel.overview: Daniel divides into two halves: six court stories of Hebrews remaining faithful under foreign empire (furnace, lions' den), and four apocalyptic visions of world empires giving way to God's eternal kingdom. The Son of Man vision (ch. 7) was central to Jesus's own self-understanding.

Hosea.author: Hosea ben Beeri
Hosea.overview: Hosea's marriage to the unfaithful Gomer becomes a living parable of God's relationship with Israel. His ministry spans Israel's final decades before Assyrian conquest, and his anguished love for his wayward wife mirrors God's persistent covenant commitment to a nation that keeps abandoning him.

Joel.author: Joel ben Pethuel
Joel.overview: A locust plague becomes the entry point for Joel's proclamation of the coming Day of the LORD — both as judgment and as the dawn of a new era when God pours his Spirit on all flesh. Peter cites Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost as the text that explains what the disciples are experiencing.

Amos.author: Amos of Tekoa
Amos.overview: Amos, a shepherd from Judah, was sent to preach to the prosperous, complacent northern kingdom of Israel. His message was radical: wealth built on oppression of the poor cannot coexist with true worship of God. His vision of justice 'rolling on like a river' shaped the prophetic tradition and the civil rights movement alike.

Obadiah.author: Obadiah
Obadiah.overview: The shortest OT book, Obadiah pronounces judgment on Edom — Israel's cousin-nation (descendants of Esau) — for gloating over Jerusalem's fall. It stands as a warning that pride in any nation's security or ancestry is misplaced, and that the day of the LORD will set all wrongs right.

Jonah.author: Unknown; set in Jonah ben Amittai's era
Jonah.date: c. 8th c. BC (setting); later composition possible
Jonah.overview: Jonah is not primarily a story about a fish but about a prophet who flees God's command to preach to Israel's enemy, Nineveh. When Nineveh repents and God relents from judgment, Jonah's anger reveals the scandal of grace — that God's mercy extends beyond Israel's borders, a truth Jonah struggles to accept.

Micah.author: Micah of Moresheth
Micah.overview: Micah alternates between oracles of judgment and promises of restoration, indicting corrupt leaders, false prophets, and economic exploitation. He distills true religion into its simplest form (6:8) and prophesies that the coming ruler of Israel will be born in Bethlehem.

Nahum.author: Nahum the Elkoshite
Nahum.overview: Where Jonah called Nineveh to repentance and they responded, Nahum — a century later — announces Nineveh's fall with no offer of reprieve. Violent Assyria, which had devastated Israel, will itself be devastated. Nahum's vision of a messenger 'bringing good news of peace' is quoted in Romans 10:15.

Habakkuk.author: Habakkuk
Habakkuk.overview: Habakkuk is structured as a dialogue — the prophet asks God why he tolerates injustice, God answers (using Babylon), Habakkuk asks again (why use a worse nation?), and God answers again. The book resolves not in explanation but in trust: 'The righteous shall live by faith' — the text Paul builds Galatians and Romans around.

Zephaniah.author: Zephaniah ben Cushi
Zephaniah.overview: Zephaniah opens with one of the most sweeping judgment oracles in all prophecy — a reversal of creation — and ends with one of the most tender restoration promises: God himself will rejoice over his people with singing. The contrast defines the prophetic movement from wrath to redemption.

Haggai.author: Haggai
Haggai.overview: Haggai's four brief messages were delivered in 520 BC to motivate the discouraged post-exilic community to resume building the Temple. His argument: their economic hardship is connected to their neglect of God's house. His vision of the Temple's future glory — greater than Solomon's — anticipates Christ's presence.

Zechariah.author: Zechariah ben Berechiah
Zechariah.overview: Zechariah combines encouraging messages for the post-exilic community with eight elaborate night visions and two major apocalyptic sections. The NT quotes Zechariah more than any other Minor Prophet — his king entering on a donkey, the thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one — all find their fulfilment in Christ.

Malachi.author: Malachi ('my messenger')
Malachi.overview: The last OT book addresses a post-exilic community grown cynical and perfunctory in worship. Using a unique disputation format, God challenges Israel's rationalizations. Malachi ends with the promise of Elijah's return before the Day of the LORD — a promise the NT sees fulfilled in John the Baptist.

Matthew.author: Matthew (Levi), apostle
Matthew.overview: Matthew is the most Jewish of the four Gospels, presenting Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's story — the new Moses, the true Israel, the long-awaited Messiah. Five major discourses (including the Sermon on the Mount) mirror the five books of Moses, and the Great Commission opens the kingdom to all nations.

Mark.author: John Mark; Peter as primary source (Papias)
Mark.overview: The shortest Gospel moves at breathtaking speed — the word 'immediately' appears 41 times. Mark presents Jesus as the suffering Servant whose identity is gradually unveiled and who must be understood through the cross. Its abrupt ending (16:8 in the earliest manuscripts) throws readers back into a world where the resurrection demands a response.

Luke.author: Luke, physician and companion of Paul
Luke.overview: Luke is the most literary of the Gospels, addressed to Theophilus as a carefully researched account. His Jesus consistently reaches toward those the religious establishment excludes — women, tax collectors, Samaritans, Gentiles. Luke and Acts form a two-volume work tracing the gospel from Bethlehem to Rome.

John.author: John the apostle (traditional); 'the Beloved Disciple'
John.overview: John's Gospel operates at a different register than the Synoptics — deeply theological, structured around seven signs and seven 'I AM' declarations. Written that readers 'may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God,' it opens in deliberate echo of Genesis: 'In the beginning was the Word.'

Acts.author: Luke, physician
Acts.overview: Acts is the sequel to Luke's Gospel, tracing the gospel's spread from Jerusalem to Rome through the Spirit-empowered witness of the early church. Its two primary figures — Peter (chs. 1–12) and Paul (chs. 13–28) — show how the good news crosses every boundary of ethnicity, class, and culture.

Romans.author: Paul
Romans.overview: Romans is Paul's most systematic exposition of the gospel — the righteousness of God revealed in the death and resurrection of Jesus for all who believe. Chapters 1–8 trace condemnation to glorification; chapters 9–11 wrestle with Israel's place in God's plan; chapters 12–16 map the ethical life of grace.

1 Corinthians.author: Paul
1 Corinthians.overview: Written to a gifted but fractured congregation in Corinth, 1 Corinthians addresses division, sexual immorality, lawsuits, idol food, worship disorder, and the resurrection. Paul's brilliant chapter on love (ch. 13) sits at the structural heart of a letter about what genuine spiritual life looks like in community.

2 Corinthians.author: Paul
2 Corinthians.overview: The most personal of Paul's letters, 2 Corinthians is a passionate defense of his apostleship against rivals who questioned his authority. Its theology of suffering — that weakness is the vessel through which God's power works — is forged in the fire of Paul's own experience.

Galatians.author: Paul
Galatians.overview: Galatians is Paul's most urgent letter, written in anger and love to communities being told they must be circumcised to complete their salvation. His argument: justification is by faith alone, not works of the Law — the same faith that Abraham exercised before circumcision existed. Freedom in Christ is the gospel's gift.

Ephesians.author: Paul (some scholars: a Pauline disciple)
Ephesians.overview: Ephesians operates on the grandest scale of any Pauline letter — God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ, gathering Jews and Gentiles into one body. The second half applies this cosmic vision to household life, community ethics, and spiritual warfare. The armor of God (ch. 6) is armor for a community, not just an individual.

Philippians.author: Paul
Philippians.overview: Written from prison, Philippians is Paul's warmest letter — full of joy, partnership language, and personal affection. The great Christ-hymn (2:6-11), tracing Jesus's descent into servanthood and exaltation, provides the theological foundation for Paul's call to humble, others-centered living.

Colossians.author: Paul (some scholars: a Pauline disciple)
Colossians.overview: Colossians counters a 'philosophy' that diminished Christ by adding angelic intermediaries and ascetic practices. Paul's response: in Christ 'all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form' — nothing needs to be added to him. The second half grounds this high Christology in everyday relationships.

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul
1 Thessalonians.overview: Probably Paul's earliest surviving letter, 1 Thessalonians pastors a young congregation anxious about believers who have died before Christ's return. Paul reassures them with the church's first detailed account of the resurrection and return of Christ, and calls them to lives of holiness while they wait.

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul (some scholars debate authenticity)
2 Thessalonians.overview: 2 Thessalonians corrects a misunderstanding that the Day of the LORD had already arrived, describing events that must first occur (the 'man of lawlessness'). It also addresses members who, expecting the imminent end, had stopped working — with Paul's blunt counter: 'If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.'

1 Timothy.author: Paul
1 Timothy.overview: The first of Paul's Pastoral Letters, 1 Timothy guides a young leader managing a congregation beset by false teachers and disorder. It covers qualifications for elders and deacons, proper worship, the role of women, care for widows, and the danger of wealth — the nuts and bolts of healthy church life.

2 Timothy.author: Paul
2 Timothy.overview: Paul's final letter, written from prison as he awaits execution, is his most personal farewell. He urges Timothy to guard the gospel, endure suffering, and trust in Scripture's power to equip for every good work (3:16-17). Its tone is both urgent and peaceful — a dying man sure of what he has believed.

Titus.author: Paul
Titus.overview: Written to Titus organizing the church in Crete, this brief letter connects sound doctrine with transformed behavior. Paul's great summary of the gospel (2:11-14) — grace training us to renounce ungodliness — grounds the practical instructions in the good news rather than mere moralism.

Philemon.author: Paul
Philemon.overview: The most personal of Paul's letters, Philemon appeals for the slave Onesimus to be received back — no longer as a slave but as 'a dear brother.' Paul stops short of demanding Onesimus's freedom but the logic of Christian brotherhood points unmistakably in that direction, planting a seed that would eventually abolish slavery.

Hebrews.author: Unknown; Paul, Apollos, Priscilla, and Barnabas all proposed
Hebrews.overview: Hebrews is a sophisticated theological sermon urging Jewish-Christian readers not to drift back into Judaism. Its argument: Jesus is superior to angels, Moses, the Levitical priesthood, and the old covenant — he is the final, perfect high priest whose sacrifice accomplishes what the tabernacle only foreshadowed. Its hall of faith (ch. 11) is the greatest meditation on faith in all Scripture.

James.author: James, brother of Jesus
James.overview: James is the most practical book of the NT, functioning like a Christian Proverbs. Its famous challenge — 'Faith without works is dead' — is not a contradiction of Paul but a challenge to a different error: using grace as a license for moral indifference. James insists that genuine faith transforms how we speak, act, and treat the poor.

1 Peter.author: Peter the apostle; Silas as scribe
1 Peter.overview: Written to scattered Christians facing social hostility across Asia Minor, 1 Peter calls them to embrace their identity as 'a holy nation, a royal priesthood' and to live such good lives among the pagans that even their suffering becomes a witness. The letter draws deeply on Isaiah's Servant Songs.

2 Peter.author: Peter the apostle (some scholars debate)
2 Peter.overview: 2 Peter warns against false teachers who exploit believers and deny Christ's return. Its description of Scripture's divine origin (1:20-21) and its cosmic vision of the Day of the LORD and the new heavens and earth make it a foundational document for Christian epistemology and eschatology.

1 John.author: John the apostle
1 John.overview: 1 John is a pastoral letter addressing a community shattered by a split — some have left, denying that Jesus came in the flesh. John's response weaves together tests of genuine faith: right belief about Jesus, love for fellow believers, and keeping God's commands. 'God is love' (4:8) is perhaps the most loaded theological statement in all Scripture.

2 John.author: John the apostle ('the Elder')
2 John.overview: This brief letter to 'the chosen lady and her children' (a congregation) warns against welcoming traveling teachers who deny the incarnation of Christ. It balances the command to love with the command to guard truth — hospitality without discernment enables error.

3 John.author: John the apostle ('the Elder')
3 John.overview: Addressed to Gaius, 3 John commends generous hospitality toward traveling missionaries and rebukes Diotrephes — a domineering leader who refuses to welcome them. It is the most private letter in the NT and one of the clearest NT glimpses of early church leadership tensions.

Jude.author: Jude, brother of Jesus
Jude.overview: Jude is an urgent call to 'contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints' against teachers who have crept in and turned grace into a license for immorality. Drawing on Jewish apocalyptic tradition, Jude lines up historical examples of God's judgment on similar rebellions, ending with one of the NT's greatest doxologies.

Revelation.author: John the apostle (traditional) or a different John
Revelation.overview: Revelation is addressed to seven real congregations under Roman imperial pressure — it is a pastoral letter written in the apocalyptic genre, using symbolic language to declare that Caesar is not lord, Christ is. Its visions of judgment and cosmic warfare ultimately culminate in the New Jerusalem — God dwelling with humanity forever, all things made new.
